dedupe_keys.name: sub saharan africa universal electrification of rural health facilities with stand alone photovoltaics

description: This case study estimates what it would cost to electrify rural health facilities across sub-Saharan Africa with decentralised solar photovoltaic systems, as a pandemic response with long-term benefits for medical equipment and communities. The authors, led by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre, published it as an open-access journal article. They mapped health facilities and their electrification status, analysed the cost of a stand-alone photovoltaic system for each location including operating costs, and combined accessibility and population distribution to estimate how many people would gain faster access to electrified care. Coverage is sub-Saharan Africa. The article is free under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Caveats: electrification status and facility inventories are incomplete, costs are modelled, not tendered, and travel time gains assume every facility is electrified. The study found a large electrification gap and put the upfront investment for more than 50,000 facilities without electricity, mostly primary health posts, at 484 million euros, with 281 million people able to cut travel time to an electrified facility by 50 minutes on average. Simulation uses: investment appraisal of health facility energy resilience and linking healthcare access models to energy supply. Related records: the Ghana health facility mini-grid study (case_study-ghana-health-facility-solar-mini-grids) and the sub-Saharan Africa public health facilities list (data-ssa-public-health-facilities) are closely related.
